name: unc3753
iocPatterns: Email lures without attachments or links
Physical infiltration by impersonated IT technicians
USB data exfiltration via removable media
Use of privnote.com for command delivery
Automated download of installers using command‑line cURL
Installation of screen‑sharing and remote support applications
Remote desktop or remote support software exploitation
Local data staging in Downloads/Roaming directories
Exfiltration to consumer cloud storage via WinSCP, Rclone, FTP/SFTP
keyCapabilities: Remote control via screen sharing and RMM tools (Zoom, Teams, AnyDesk, Bomgar, Zoho Assist)
Automated installation of SuperOps RMM agent through cURL/PowerShell scripts
Physical intrusion by impersonated technicians using removable USB devices for direct data theft
Targeted search and collection of sensitive documents across legal repositories (iManage), financial records, and PII
Local staging of stolen files into Downloads or roaming directories
Exfiltration to cloud storage via WinSCP, Rclone, FTP/SFTP, or consumer services like OneDrive and Google Drive
Command dissemination through self‑destroying note service privnote.com
Extortion letter production distributed shortly after data theft
Historical use of LOCKBIT.BLACK ransomware but now operating exclusively as a blackmail campaign
recommendedActions: Educate employees on vishing and verify caller identity before installing any software or granting remote access.
Implement strict usage policies for remote support tools such as AnyDesk, Bomgar, Zoom, Teams, and Zoho Assist; block unauthorized use.
Detect and monitor automated downloads via cURL or PowerShell from untrusted IPs; enforce whitelists on endpoint download activity.
Deploy controls to detect and limit communication with privnote.com for command delivery; consider network-level filtering.
Restrict BYOD device access to corporate VDI environments, requiring MFA and continuous monitoring.
Deploy DLP rules to prevent large outbound transfers via WinSCP, FTP/SFTP, or consumer cloud services like OneDrive and Google Drive.

Block consumer cloud accounts from being used as exfiltration channels unless business‑justified. Set alerts for suspicious large file uploads or outgoing connections over FTP/SFTP. Implement endpoint monitoring to flag RMM agent installations such as SuperOps; enforce whitelisting. Strengthen physical security controls—visitor check‑in, badge enforcement, and camera coverage—to deter impersonated technicians. Enforce USB device control policies with restrictive storage media handling; Conduct recurrent vishing and phishing awareness training for staff.
campaignsText: UNC3753’s attacks typically begin with a targeted vishing call that convinces the victim to install or connect to remote‑support software. Within minutes, attackers are able to walk through network shares and locate confidential files via keyword searches, staging them locally for rapid exfiltration. Most incidents unfold within a single business day and culminate in an extortion letter delivered via email or printed hard copy. The group has broadened its techniques to include physical site visits with USB‑based theft, indicating operational flexibility and a willingness to blend cyber exploitation with traditional espionage tactics.
description: UNC3753 (also known as Luna Moth, Chatty Spider and the Silent Ransom Group) is a nation‑state actor that has carried out a financially motivated data‑theft and extortion campaign against U.S. law firms and financial institutions from January to May 2026. The group leverages voice phishing, remote‑support tools, and occasional physical intrusions to exfiltrate highly sensitive documents within hours and then pressures victims with extortion letters threatening public disclosure.
goals: The primary strategic objective of UNC3753 is financial gain through blackmailing high‑profile U.S. organizations that possess large volumes of proprietary or sensitive data in sectors that generally exhibit lower readiness for social engineering attacks, such as legal and financial services. By exploiting the perceived legitimacy of an IT support pretext, the actors lower the barrier to entry and focus on exfiltrating data before a formal law‑enforcement response can be coordinated.
